passages.text: Ah! if only they had been invited to a Bacchic revelling, or a feast of Pan or Aphrodité or Genetyllis,[1] why! the streets would have been impassable for the thronging tambourines! Now there’s never a woman here—ah! except my neighbour Calonicé, whom I see approaching yonder. . . . Good day, Calonicé.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Good day, Lysistrata; but pray, why this dark, forbidding face, my dear? Believe me, you don’t look a bit pretty with those black lowering brows.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! Calonicé, my heart is on fire; I blush for our sex. Men *will* have it we are tricky and sly. . . .
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And they are quite right, upon my word!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yet, look you, when the women are summoned to meet for a matter of the last importance, they lie abed instead of coming.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! they will come, my dear; but ’tis not easy, you know, for women to leave the house. One is busy pottering about her husband; another is getting the servant up; a third is putting her child asleep, or washing the brat or feeding it.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But I tell you, the business that calls them here is far and away more urgent.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And why *do* you summon us, dear Lysistrata? What is it all about?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes indeed, both big and great.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And we are not all on the spot!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! if it were what you suppose, there would be never an absentee. No, no, it concerns a thing I have turned about and about this way and that of many sleepless nights.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: It must be something mighty fine and subtle for you to have turned it about so!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: So fine, it means just this, Greece saved by the women!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: By women! Why, its salvation hangs on a poor thread then!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Our country’s fortunes depend on us—it is with us to undo utterly the Peloponnesians. . . .
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: That would be a noble deed truly!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: To exterminate the Bœotians to a man!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But surely you would spare the eels.[3]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: For Athens’ sake I will never threaten so fell a doom; trust me for that. However, if the Bœotian and Peloponnesian women join us, Greece is saved.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But how should women perform so wise and glorious an achievement, we women who dwell in the retirement of the household, clad in diaphanous garments of yellow silk and long flowing gowns, decked out with flowers and shod with dainty little slippers?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Nay, but those are the very sheet-anchors of our salvation—those yellow tunics, those scents and slippers, those cosmetics and transparent robes.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: There is not a man will wield a lance against another . . .
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Quick, I will get me a yellow tunic from the dyer’s.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I’ll run and put on a flowing gown.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I’ll haste and buy a pair of slippers this instant.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Now tell me, would not the women have done best to come?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Why, they should have *flown* here!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! my dear, you'll see that like true Athenians, they will do everything too late.[4] . . . Why, there’s not a woman come from the shoreward parts, not one from Salamis?[5]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But I know for certain they embarked at daybreak.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And the dames from Acharnæ![6] why, I thought they would have been the very first to arrive.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Theagenes wife[7] at any rate is sure to come; she has actually been to consult Hecaté. . . . But look! here are some arrivals—and there are more behind. Ah! ha! now what countrywomen may they be?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes! upon my word, ’tis a levy *en masse* of all the female population of Anagyra!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Are we late, Lysistrata? Tell us, pray; what, not a word?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I cannot say much for you, Myrrhiné! you have not bestirred yourself overmuch for an affair of such urgency.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I could not find my girdle in the dark. However, if the matter is so pressing, here we are; so speak.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No, but let us wait a moment more, till the women of Bœotia arrive and those from the Peloponnese.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, that is best. . . . Ah! here comes Lampito.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Good day, Lampito, dear friend from Lacedæmon. How well and handsome you look! what a rosy complexion! and how strong you seem; why, you could strangle a bull surely!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, indeed, I really think I could. ’Tis because I do gymnastics and practise the kick dance.[9]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: La! you are feeling me as if I were a beast for sacrifice.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And this young woman, what countrywoman is she?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: She is a noble lady from Bœotia.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! my pretty Bœotian friend, you are as blooming as a garden.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, on my word! and the garden is so prettily weeded too![10]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: ’Tis an honest woman, by my faith! she comes from Corinth.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! honest, no doubt then—as honesty goes at Corinth.[11]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But who has called together this council of women, pray?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well then, tell us what you want of us.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What is the most important business you wish to inform us about?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I will tell you. But first answer me one question.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Don’t you feel sad and sorry because the fathers of your children are far away from you with the army? For I’ll undertake, there is not one of you whose husband is not abroad at this moment.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Mine has been the last five months in Thrace—looking after Eucrates.[12]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: ’Tis seven long months since mine left me for Pylos.[13]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: As for mine, if he ever does return from service, he’s no sooner back than he takes down his shield again and flies back to the wars.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And not so much as the shadow of a lover! Since the day the Milesians betrayed us, I have never once seen an eight-inch-long *godemiche* even, to be a leathern consolation to us poor widows. . . . Now tell me, if I have discovered a means of ending the war, will you all second me?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes verily, by all the goddesses, I swear I will, though I have to put my gown in pawn, and drink the money the same day.[14]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And so will I, though I must be split in two like a flat-fish, and have half myself removed.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And I too; why, to secure Peace, I would climb to the top of Mount Taygetus.[15]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Then I will out with it at last, my mighty secret! Oh! sister women, if we would compel our husbands to make peace, we must refrain . . .
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Refrain from what? tell us, tell us!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: We will, we will, though we should die of it.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: We must refrain from the male organ altogether. . . . Nay, why do you turn your backs on me? Where are you going? So, you bite your lips, and shake your heads, eh? Why these pale, sad looks? why these tears? Come, will you do it—yes or no? Do you hesitate?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No, I will not do it; let the War go on.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And you, my pretty flat-fish, who declared just now they might split you in two?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Anything, anything but that! Bid me go through the fire, if you will; but to rob us of the sweetest thing in all the world, my dear, dear Lysistrata!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, I agree with the others; I too would sooner go through the fire.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh, wanton, vicious sex! the poets have done well to make tragedies upon us; we are good for nothing then but love and lewdness![16] But you, my dear, you from hardy Sparta, if *you* join me, all may yet be well; help me, second me, I conjure you.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: ’Tis a hard thing, by the two goddesses[17] it is! for a woman to sleep alone without ever a standing weapon in her bed. But there, Peace must come first.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh, my dear, my dearest, best friend, you are the only one deserving the name of woman!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But if—which the gods forbid—we do refrain altogether from what you say, should we get peace any sooner?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Of course we should, by the goddesses twain! We need only sit indoors with painted cheeks, and meet our mates lightly clad in transparent gowns of Amorgos[18] silk, and with our “mottes” nicely plucked smooth; then their tools will stand like mad and they will be wild to lie with us. That will be the time to refuse, and they will hasten to make peace, I am convinced of that!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, just as Menelaus, when he saw Helen’s naked bosom, threw away his sword, they say.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But, poor devils, suppose our husbands go away and leave us.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Then, as Pherecrates says, we must “flay a skinned dog,”[19] that’s all.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Bah! these proverbs are all idle talk. . . . But if our husbands drag us by main force into the bedchamber?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Then yield to their wishes, but with a bad grace; there is no pleasure for them, when they do it by force. Besides, there are a thousand ways of tormenting them. Never fear, they'll soon tire of the game; there’s no satisfaction for a man, unless the woman shares it.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Very well, if you *will* have it so, we agree.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: For ourselves, no doubt we shall persuade our husbands to conclude a fair and honest peace; but there is the Athenian populace, how are we to cure these folk of their warlike frenzy?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! but we have seen to that; this very day the Acropolis will be in our hands. That is the task assigned to the older women; while we are here in council, they are going, under pretence of offering sacrifice, to seize the citadel.

passages.text: ’Tis what I was telling you; the women have just occupied the Acropolis. So now, Lampito, do you return to Sparta to organize the plot, while your comrades here remain as hostages. For ourselves, let us away to join the rest in the citadel, and let us push the bolts well home.

passages.text: Go easy, Draces, go easy; why, your shoulder is all chafed by these plaguey heavy olive stocks. But forward still, forward, man, as needs must. What unlooked-for things do happen, to be sure, in a long life! Ah! Strymodorus, who would ever have thought it? Here we have the women, who used, for our misfortune, to eat our bread and live in our houses, daring nowadays to lay hands on the holy image of the goddess, to seize the Acropolis and draw bars and bolts to keep any from entering! Come, Philurgus man, let’s hurry thither; let’s lay our faggots all about the citadel, and on the blazing pile burn with our hands these vile conspiratresses, one and all—and Lycon’s wife, Lysistrata, first and foremost! Nay, by Demeter, never will I let ’em laugh at me, whiles I have a breath left in my body. Cleomenes himself,[24] the first who ever seized our citadel, had to quit it to his sore dishonour; spite his Lacedæmonian pride, he had to deliver me up his arms and slink off with a single garment to his back. My word! but he was filthy and ragged! and what an unkempt beard, to be sure! He had not had a bath for six long years! Oh! but that was a mighty siege! Our men were ranged seventeen deep before the gate, and never left their posts, even to sleep. These women, these enemies of Euripides and all the gods, shall I do nothing to hinder their inordinate insolence? else let them tear down my trophies of Marathon. But look ye, to finish our toilsome climb, we have only this last steep bit left to mount. Verily ’tis no easy job without beasts of burden, and how these logs do bruise my shoulder! Still let us on, and blow up our fire and see it does not go out just as we reach our destination. Phew! phew! (*blows the fire*). Oh! dear! what a dreadful smoke! it bites my eyes like a mad dog. It is Lemnos[25] fire for sure, or it would never devour my eyelids like this. Come on, Laches, let’s hurry, let’s bring succour to the goddess; it’s now or never! Phew! phew! (*blows the fire*). Oh! dear! what a confounded smoke!—There now, there’s our fire all bright and burning, thank the gods! Now, why not first put down our loads here, then take a vine-branch, light it at the brazier and hurl it at the gate by way of battering-ram? If they don’t answer our summons by pulling back the bolts, then we set fire to the woodwork, and the smoke will choke ’em. Ye gods! what a smoke! Pfaugh! Is there never a Samos general will help me unload my burden?[26]—Ah! it shall not gall my shoulder any more. (*Tosses down his wood*.) Come, brazier, do your duty, make the embers flare, that I may kindle a brand; I want to be the first to hurl one. Aid me, heavenly Victory; let us punish for their insolent audacity the women who have seized our citadel, and may we raise a trophy of triumph for success!
