passages.text: Oh! my dears, methinks I see fire and smoke; can it be a conflagration? Let us hurry all we can. Fly, fly, Nicodicé, ere Calycé and Crityllé perish in the fire, or are stifled in the smoke raised by these accursed old men and their pitiless laws. But, great gods, can it be I come too late? Rising at dawn, I had the utmost trouble to fill this vessel at the fountain. Oh! what a crowd there was, and what a din! What a rattling of water-pots! Servants and slave-girls pushed and thronged me! However, here I have it full at last; and I am running to carry the water to my fellow townswomen, whom our foes are plotting to burn alive. News has been brought us that a company of old, doddering greybeards, loaded with enormous faggots, as if they wanted to heat a furnace, have taken the field, vomiting dreadful threats, crying that they must reduce to ashes these horrible women. Suffer them not, oh! goddess, but, of thy grace, may I see Athens and Greece cured of their warlike folly. ’Tis to this end, oh! thou guardian deity of our city, goddess of the golden crest, that they have seized thy sanctuary. Be their friend and ally, Athené, and if any man hurl against them lighted firebrands, aid us to carry water to extinguish them.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Let me be, I say. Oh! oh! (*She calls for help*.)
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What is this I see, ye wretched old men? Honest and pious folk ye cannot be who act so vilely.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah, ha! here’s something new! a swarm of women stand posted outside to defend the gates!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! ah! we frighten you, do we; we seem a mighty host, yet you do not see the ten-thousandth part of our sex.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ho, Phædrias! shall we stop their cackle? Suppose one of us were to break a stick across their backs, eh?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Let us set down our water-pots on the ground, to be out of the way, if they should dare to offer us violence.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Let. someone knock out two or three teeth for them, as they did to Bupalus;[28] they won’t talk so loud then.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Come on then; I wait you with unflinching foot, and I will snap off your testicles like a bitch.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Silence! ere my stick has cut short your days.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Now, just you dare to touch Stratyllis with the tip of your finger!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And if I batter you to pieces with my fists, what will you do?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I will tear out your lungs and entrails with my teeth.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! what a clever poet is Euripides! how well he says that woman is the most shameless of animals.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Let’s pick up our water-jars again, Rhodippé.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! accursed harlot, what do you mean to do here with your water?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And you, old death-in-life, with your fire? Is it to cremate yourself?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I am going to build you a pyre to roast your female friends upon.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And I,—I am going to put out your fire.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I don’t know what prevents me from roasting you with this torch.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I am getting you a bath ready to clean off the filth.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: A bath for me, you dirty slut, you!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, indeed, a nuptial bath—he, he!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Do you hear that? What insolence!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I am a free woman, I tell you.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I will make you hold your tongue, never fear!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah, ha! you shall never sit more amongst the heliasts.[29]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Water, do your office! (*The women pitch the water in their water-pots over the old men*.)
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Hot, great gods! Enough, enough!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I’m watering you, to make you bloom afresh.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Alas! I am too dry! Ah, me! how I am trembling with cold!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: These women, have they made din enough, I wonder, with their tambourines? bewept Adonis enough upon their terraces?[30] I was listening to the speeches last assembly day,[31] and Demostratus,[32] whom heaven confound! was saying we must all go over to Sicily—and lo! his wife was dancing round repeating: Alas! alas! Adonis, woe is me for Adonis!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Demostratus was saying we must levy hoplites at Zacynthus[33]—and lo! his wife, more than half drunk, was screaming on the house-roof: “Weep, weep for Adonis!”—while that infamous *Mad Ox*[34] was bellowing away on his side.—Do ye not blush, ye women, for your wild and uproarious doings?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But you don’t know all their effrontery yet! They abused and insulted us; then soused us with the water in their water-pots, and have set us wringing out our clothes, for all the world as if we had bepissed ourselves.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And ’tis well done too, by Poseidon! We men must share the blame of their ill conduct; it is we who teach them to love riot and dissoluteness and sow the seeds of wickedness in their hearts. You see a husband go into a shop: “Look you, jeweller,” says he, “you remember the necklace you made for my wife. Well, t’other evening, when she was dancing, the catch came open. Now, I am bound to start for Salamis; will you make it convenient to go up to-night to make her fastening secure?” Another will go to a cobbler, a great, strong fellow, with a great, long tool, and tell him: “The strap of one of my wife’s sandals presses her little toe, which is extremely sensitive; come in about midday to supple the thing and stretch it.” Now see the results. Take my own case—as a Magistrate I have enlisted rowers; I want money to pay ’em, and lo! the women clap to the door in my face.[35] But why do we stand here with arms crossed? Bring me a crowbar; I’ll chastise their insolence!—Ho! there, my fine fellow! (*addressing one of his attendant officers*) what are you gaping at the crows about? looking for a tavern, I suppose, eh? Come, crowbars here, and force open the gates. I will put a hand to the work myself.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No need to force the gates; I am coming out—here I am. And why bolts and bars? What we want here is not bolts and bars and locks, but common sense.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Really, my fine lady! Where is my officer? I want him to tie that woman’s hands behind her back.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: By Artemis, the virgin goddess! if he touches me with the tip of his finger, officer of the public peace though he be, let him look out for himself!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Magistrate (*to the officer*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: How now, are you afraid? Seize her, I tell you, round the body. Two of you at her, and have done with it!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: By Pandrosos! if you lay a hand on her, I'll trample you underfoot till you shit your guts!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh, there! my guts! Where is my other officer? Bind that minx first, who speaks so prettily!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: By Phœbé, if you touch her with one finger, you’d better call quick for a surgeon!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What do you mean? Officer, where are you got to? Lay hold of her. Oh! but I’m going to stop your foolishness for you all!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: By the Tauric Artemis, if you go near her, I’ll pull out your hair, scream as you like.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! miserable man that I am! My own officers desert me. What ho! are we to let ourselves be bested by a mob of women? Ho! Scythians mine, close up your ranks, and forward!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: By the holy goddesses! you’ll have to make acquaintance with four companies of women, ready for the fray and well armed to boot.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Forward, Scythians, and bind them!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Forward, my gallant companions; march forth, ye vendors of grain and eggs, garlic and vegetables, keepers of taverns and bakeries, wrench and strike and tear; come, a torrent of invective and insult! (*They beat the officers*.) Enough, enough! now retire, never rob the vanquished!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Here’s a fine exploit for my officers!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah, ha! so you thought you had only to do with a set of slave-women! you did not know the ardour that fills the bosom of free-born dames.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ardour! yes, by Apollo, ardour enough—especially for the wine-cup!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Sir, sir! what use of words? they are of no avail with wild beasts of this sort. Don’t you know how they have just washed us down—and with no very fragrant soap!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What would you have? You should never have laid rash hands on us. If you start afresh, I'll knock your eyes out. My delight is to stay at home as coy as a young maid, without hurting anybody or moving any more than a milestone; but ware the wasps, if you go stirring up the wasps’ nest!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! great gods! how get the better of these ferocious creatures? ’tis past all bearing! But come, let us try to find out the reason of the dreadful scourge. With what end in view have they seized the citadel of Cranaus,[36] the sacred shrine that is raised upon the inaccessible rock of the Acropolis? Question them; be cautious and not too credulous. ’Twould be culpable negligence not to pierce the mystery, if we may.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Magistrate (*addressing the women*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I would ask you first why ye have barred our gates.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: To seize the treasury; no more money, no more war.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Then money is the cause of the War?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And of all our troubles. ’Twas to find occasion to steal that Pisander[37] and all the other agitators were for ever raising revolutions. Well and good! but they’ll never get another drachma here.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What do you propose to do then, pray?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You ask me that! Why, we propose to administer the treasury ourselves.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What is there in that to surprise you? Do we not administer the budget of household expenses?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But that is not the same thing.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: It is the treasury supplies the expenses of the War.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: That’s our first principle—no War!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What! and the safety of the city?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, we’re going to save you, whether you will or no.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! the impudence of the creatures!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You seem annoyed! but there, you’ve got to come to it.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But ’tis the very height of iniquity!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: We’re going to save you, my man.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But if I don’t want to be saved?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But what a notion, to concern yourselves with questions of Peace and War!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Out with it then; quick, or . . . (*threatening her*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Listen, and never a movement, please!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! it is too much for me! I cannot keep my temper!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Then look out for yourself; you have more to fear than we have.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Stop your croaking, old crow, you! (*To Lysistrata*.) Now you, say your say.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Willingly. All the long time the War has lasted, we have endured in modest silence all you men did; we never allowed ourselves to open our lips. We were far from satisfied, for we knew how things were going; often in our homes we would hear you discussing, upside down and inside out, some important turn of affairs. Then with sad hearts, but smiling lips, we would ask you: Well, in to-day’s Assembly did they vote Peace?—But, “Mind your own business!” the husband would growl, “Hold your tongue, do!” And I would say no more.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I would not have held my tongue though, not I!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You would have been reduced to silence by blows then.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, for my part, I would say no more. But presently I would come to know you had arrived at some fresh decision more fatally foolish than ever. “Ah! my dear man,” I would say, “what madness next!” But he would only look at me askance and say: “Just weave your web, do; else your cheeks will smart for hours. War is men’s business!”
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: How now, wretched man? not to let us contend against your follies, was bad enough! But presently we heard you asking out loud in the open street: “Is there never a man left in Athens?” and, “No, not one, not one,” you were assured in reply. Then, then we made up our minds without more delay to make common cause to save Greece. Open your ears to our wise counsels and hold your tongues, and we may yet put things on a better footing.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You put things indeed! Oh! ’tis too much! The insolence of the creatures! Silence, I say.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: May I die a thousand deaths ere I obey one who wears a veil!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: If that’s all that troubles you, here, take my veil, wrap it round your head, and hold your tongue. Then take this basket; put on a girdle, card wool, munch beans. The War shall be women’s business.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Lay aside your water-pots, we will guard them, we will help our friends and companions. For myself, I will never weary of the dance; my knees will never grow stiff with fatigue. I will brave everything with my dear allies, on whom Nature has lavished virtue, grace, boldness, cleverness, and whose wisely directed energy is going to save the State. Oh! my good, gallant Lysistrata, and all my friends, be ever like a bundle of nettles; never let your anger slacken; the winds of fortune blow our way.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: May gentle Love and the sweet Cyprian Queen shower seductive charms on our bosoms and all our person. If only we may stir so amorous a lust among the men that their tools stand stiff as sticks, we shall indeed deserve the name of peace-makers among the Greeks.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: To begin with, we shall not see you any more running like mad fellows to the Market holding lance in fist.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: That will be something gained, anyway, by the Paphian goddess, it will!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Now we see ’em, mixed up with saucepans and kitchen stuff, armed to the teeth, looking like wild Corybantes![38]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Why, of course; that’s how brave men should do.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! but what a funny sight, to behold a man wearing a Gorgon’s-head buckler coming along to buy fish!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: ’Tother day in the Market I saw a phylarch[39] with flowing ringlets; he was a-horseback, and was pouring into his helmet the broth he had just bought att an old dame’s stall. There was a Thracian warrior too, who was brandishing his lance like Tereus in the play;[40] he had scared a good woman selling figs into a perfect panic, and was gobbling up all her ripest fruit.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And how, pray, would you propose to restore peace and order in all the countries of Greece?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: ’Tis the easiest thing in the world!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Come, tell us how; I am curious to know.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: When we are winding thread, and it is tangled, we pass the spool across and through the skein, now this way, now that way; even so, to finish off the War, we shall send embassies hither and thither and everywhere, to disentangle matters.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And ’tis with your yarn, and your skeins, and your spools, you think to appease so many bitter enmities, you silly women?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: If only you had common sense, you would always do in politics the same as we do with our yarn.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: First we wash the yarn to separate the grease and filth; do the same with all bad citizens, sort them out and drive them forth with rods—’tis the refuse of the city. Then for all such as come crowding up in search of employments and offices, we must card them thoroughly; then, to bring them all to the same standard, pitch them pell-mell into the same basket, resident aliens or no, allies, debtors to the State, all mixed up together. Then as for our Colonies, you must think of them as so many isolated hanks; find the ends of the separate threads, draw them to a centre here, wind them into one, make one great hank of the lot, out of which the Public can weave itself a good, stout tunic.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Is it not a sin and a shame to see them carding and winding the State, these women who have neither art nor part in the burdens of the War?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What! wretched man! why, ’tis a far heavier burden to us than to you. In the first place, we bear sons who go off to fight far away from Athens.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Enough said! do not recall sad and sorry memories![41]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Then secondly, instead of enjoying the pleasures of love and making the best. of our youth and beauty, we are left to languish far from our husbands, who are all with the army. But say no more of ourselves; what afflicts me is to see our girls growing old in lonely grief.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: That is not the same thing. When the soldier returns from the wars, even though he has white hair, he very soon finds a young wife. But a woman has only one summer; if she does not make hay while the sun shines, no one will afterwards have anything to say to her, and she spends her days consulting oracles, that never send her a husband.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But the old man who can still erect his organ . . .
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But you, why don’t you get done with it and die? You are rich; go buy yourself a bier, and I will knead you a honey-cake for Cerberus. Here, take this garland. (*Drenching him with water*.)
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And this one too. (*Drenching him with water*.)
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And these fillets. (*Drenching him with water*.)
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What do you lack more? Step aboard the boat; Charon is waiting for you, you're keeping him from pushing off.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: To treat me so scurvily! What an insult! I will go show myself to my fellow-magistrates just as I am.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What! are you blaming us for not having exposed you according to custom?[42] Nay, console yourself; we will not fail to offer up the third-day sacrifice for you, first thing in the morning.[43]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Awake, friends of freedom; let us hold ourselves aye ready to act. I suspect a mighty peril; I foresee another Tyranny like Hippias’.[44] I am sore afraid the Laconians assembled here with Cleisthenes have, by a stratagem of war, stirred up these women, enemies of the gods, to seize upon our treasury and the funds whereby I lived.[45] Is it not a sin and a shame for them to interfere in advising the citizens, to prate of shields and lances, and to ally themselves with Laconians, fellows I trust no more than I would so many famished wolves? The whole thing, my friends, is nothing else but an attempt to re-establish Tyranny. But I will never submit; I will be on my guard for the future; I will always. carry a blade hidden under myrtle boughs; I will post myself in the Public Square under arms, shoulder to shoulder with Aristogiton;[46] and now, to make a start, I must just break a few of that cursed old jade’s teeth yonder.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Nay, never play the brave man, else when you go back home, your own mother won’t know you. But, dear friends and allies, first let us lay our burdens down; then, citizens all, hear what I have to say. I have useful counsel to give our city, which deserves it well at my hands for the brilliant distinctions it has lavished on my girlhood. At seven years of age, I was bearer of the sacred vessels; at ten, I pounded barley for the altar of Athené; next, clad in a robe of yellow silk, I was *little bear* to Artemis at the Brauronia;[47] presently, grown a tall, handsome maiden, they put a necklace of dried figs about my neck, and I was Basket-Bearer.[48] So surely I am bound to give my best advice to Athens. What matters that I was born a woman, if I can cure your misfortunes? I pay my share of tolls and taxes, by giving men to the State. But you, you miserable greybeards, you contribute nothing to the public charges; on the contrary, you have wasted the treasure of our forefathers, as it was called, the treasure amassed in the days of the Persian Wars.[49] You pay nothing at all in return; and into the bargain you endanger our lives and liberties by your mistakes. Have you one word to say for yourselves? . . . Ah! don’t irritate me, you there, or I'll lay my slipper across your jaws; and it’s pretty heavy.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Outrage upon outrage! things are going from bad to worse. Let us punish the minxes, every one of us that has a man’s appendages to boast of. Come, off with our tunics, for a man must savour of manhood; come, my friends, let us strip naked from head to foot. Courage, I say, we who in our day garrisoned Lipsydrion;[50] let us be young again, and shake off eld. If we give them the least hold over us, ’tis all up! their audacity will know no bounds! We shall see them building ships, and fighting sea-fights, like Artemisia;[51] nay, if they want to mount and ride as cavalry, we had best cashier the knights, for indeed women excel in riding, and have a fine, firm seat for the gallop.[52] Just think of all those squadrons of Amazons Micon has painted for us engaged in hand-to-hand combat with men.[53] Come then, we must e’en fit collars to all these willing necks.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: By the blessed goddesses, if you anger me, I will let loose the beast of my evil passions, and a very hailstorm of blows will set you yelling for help. Come, dames, off tunics, and quick’s the word; women must scent the savour of women in the throes of passion. . . . Now just you dare to measure strength with me, old greybeard, and I warrant you you’ll never eat garlic or black beans more. No, not a word! my anger is at boiling point, and I’ll do with you what the beetle did with the eagle’s eggs.[54] I laugh at your threats, so long as I have on my side Lampito here, and the noble Theban, my dear Ismenia. . . . Pass decree on decree, you can do us no hurt, you wretch abhorred of all your fellows. Why, only yesterday, on occasion of the feast of Hecaté, I asked my neighbours of Bœotia for one of their daughters for whom my girls have a lively liking—a fine, fat eel to wit; and if they did not refuse, all along of your silly decrees! We shall never cease to suffer the like, till someone gives you a neat trip-up and breaks your neck for you!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Chorus of Women (*addressing Lysistrata*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You, Lysistrata, you who are leader of our glorious enterprise, why do I see you coming towards me with so gloomy an air?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: ’Tis the behaviour of these naughty women, ’tis the female heart and female weakness so discourages me.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What has happened so disconcerting; come, tell your friends.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! the thing is so hard to tell—yet so impossible to conceal.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Nay, never seek to hide any ill that has befallen our cause.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: To blurt it out in a word—we are in heat!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What use calling upon Zeus? The thing is even as I say. I cannot stop them any longer from lusting after the men. They are all for deserting. The first I caught was slipping out by the postern gate near the cave of Pan; another was letting herself down by a rope and pulley; a third was busy preparing her escape; while a fourth, perched on a bird’s back, was just taking wing for Orsilochus’ house,[55] when I seized her by the hair. One and all, they are inventing excuses to be off home. Look! there goes one, trying to get out! Halloa there! whither away so fast?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I want to go home; I have some Miletus wool in the house, which is getting all eaten up by the worms.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Bah! you and your worms! go back, I say!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I will return immediately, I swear I will by the two goddesses! I only have just to spread it out on the bed.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You shall not do anything of the kind! I say, you shall not go.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Must I leave my wool to spoil then?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Unhappy woman that I am! Alas for my flax! I’ve left it at home unstript!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: So, here’s another trying to escape to go home and strip her flax forsooth!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! I swear by the goddess of light, the instant I have put it in condition I will come straight back.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You shall do nothing of the kind! If once you began, others would want to follow suit.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! goddess divine, Ilithyia, patroness of women in labour, stay, stay the birth, till I have reached a spot less hallowed than Athené’s Mount!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What mean you by these silly tales?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I am going to have a child—now, this minute.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But you were not pregnant yesterday!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, I am to-day. Oh! let me go in search of the midwife, Lysistrata, quick, quick!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What is this fable you are telling me? Ah! what have you got there so hard?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No, no, by Aphrodité! nothing of the sort! Why, it feels like something hollow—a pot or a kettle. Oh! you baggage, if you have not got the sacred helmet of Pallas—and you said you were with child!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: For fear my pains should seize me in the Acropolis; I mean to lay my eggs in this helmet, as the doves do.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Excuses and pretences every word! the thing’s as clear as daylight. Anyway, you must stay here now till the fifth day, your day of purification.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I cannot sleep any more in the Acropolis, now I have seen the snake that guards the Temple.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! and those confounded owls with their dismal hooting! I cannot get a wink of rest, and I’m just dying of fatigue.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You wicked women, have done with your falsehoods! You want your husbands, that’s plain enough. But don’t you think they want you just as badly? They are spending dreadful nights, oh! I know that well enough. But hold out, my dears, hold out! A little more patience, and the victory will be ours. An Oracle promises us success, if only we remain united. Shall I repeat the words?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, tell us what the Oracle declares.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Silence then! Now—“Whenas the swallows, fleeing before the hoopoes, shall have all flocked together in one place, and shall refrain them from all amorous commerce, then will be the end of all the ills of life; yea, and Zeus, which doth thunder in the skies, shall set above what was erst below. . . .”
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What! shall the men be underneath?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: “But if dissension do arise among the swallows, and they take wing from the holy Temple, ’twill be said there is never a more wanton bird in all the world.”
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ye gods! the prophecy is clear. Nay, never let us be cast down by calamity! let us be brave to bear, and go back to our posts. ’Twere shameful indeed not to trust the promises of the Oracle.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I want to tell you a fable they used to relate to me when I was a little boy. This is it: Once upon a time there was a young man called Melanion, who hated the thought of marriage so sorely that he fled away to the wilds. So he dwelt in the mountains, wove himself nets, kept a dog and caught hares. He never, never came back, he had such a horror of women. As chaste as Melanion,[56] we loathe the jades just as much as he did.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You dear old woman, I would fain kiss you.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I will set you crying without onions.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: . . . And give you a sound kicking.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah, ha! what a dense forest you have there! (*Pointing*.)
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: So was Myronides one of the best-bearded of men o’ this side; his backside was all black, and he terrified his enemies as much as Phormio.[57]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I want to tell you a fable too, to match yours about Melanion. Once there was a certain man called Timon,[58] a tough customer, and a whimsical, a true son of the Furies, with a face that seemed to glare out of a thorn-bush. He withdrew from the world because he couldn’t abide bad men, after vomiting a thousand curses at ’em, He had a holy horror of ill-conditioned fellows, but he was mighty tender towards women.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Suppose I up and broke your jaw for you!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Suppose I let fly a good kick at you?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I should see your backside then.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You would see that, for all my age, it is very well attended to, and all fresh singed smooth.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ho there! come quick, come quick!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: A man! a man! I see him approaching all afire with the flames of love. Oh! divine Queen of Cyprus, Paphos and Cythera, I pray you still be propitious to our emprise.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Where is he, this unknown foe?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yonder—beside the Temple of Demeter.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, indeed, I see him; but who is it?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Look, look! does any of you recognize him?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I do, I do! ’tis my husband Cinesias.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: To work then! Be it your task to inflame and torture and torment him. Seductions, caresses, provocations, refusals, try every means! Grant every favour,—always excepting what is forbidden by our oath on the wine-bowl.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Have no fear, I undertake the work.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, I will stay here to help you cajole the man and set his passions aflame. The rest of you, withdraw.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Alas! alas! how I am tortured by spasm and rigid convulsion! Oh! I am racked on the wheel!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Who is this that dares to pass our lines?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, no doubt about it, a man!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But who are you that thus repulses me?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: By all the gods, call Myrrhiné hither.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Call Myrrhiné hither, quotha? And pray, who are you?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I am her husband, Cinesias, son of Peon.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! good day, my dear friend. Your name is not unknown amongst us. Your wife has it for ever on her lips; and she never touches an egg or an apple without saying: “’Twill be for Cinesias.”
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, indeed, by Aphrodité! And if we fall to talking of men, quick your wife declares: “Oh! all the rest, they’re good for nothing compared with Cinesias.”
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! I beseech you, go and call her to me.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And what will you give me for my trouble?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: This, if you like (*handling his tool*). I will give you what I have there!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, well, I will tell her to come.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Quick, oh! be quick! Life has no more charms for me since she left my house. I am sad, sad, when I go indoors; it all seems so empty; my victuals have lost their savour. Desire is eating out my heart!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I love him, oh! I love him; but he won’t let himself be loved. No! I shall not come.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Myrrhiné, my little darling Myrrhiné, what are you saying? Come down to me quick.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I call you, Myrrhiné, Myrrhiné; will you not come?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Why should you call me? You do not want me.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Not want you! Why, my weapon stands stiff with desire!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! Myrrhiné, Myrrhiné, in our child’s name, hear me; at any rate hear the child! Little lad, call your mother.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: There, listen! Don’t you pity the poor child? It’s six days now you’ve never washed and never fed the child.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Poor darling, your father takes mighty little care of you!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Come down, dearest, come down for the child’s sake.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! what a thing it is to be a mother! Well, well, we must come down, I suppose.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Why, how much younger and prettier she looks! And how she looks at me so lovingly! Her cruelty and scorn only redouble my passion.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You are as sweet as your father is provoking! Let me kiss you, my treasure, mother’s darling!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! what a bad thing it is to let yourself be led away by other women! Why give me such pain and suffering, and yourself into the bargain?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Everything is going to rack and ruin in the house.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But your web that’s all being pecked to pieces by the cocks and hens, don’t you care for that?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And Aphrodité, whose mysteries you have not celebrated for so long? Oh! won’t you come back home?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No, at least, not till a sound Treaty put an end to the War.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, if you wish it so much, why, we'll make it, your Treaty.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well and good! When that’s done, I will come home. Till then, I am bound by an oath.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: At any rate, let’s have a short time together.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No, no, no! . . . all the same I cannot say I don’t love you.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You love me? Then why refuse what I ask, my little girl, my sweet Myrrhiné.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You must be joking! What, before the child!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Manes, carry the lad home. There, you see, the child is gone; there’s nothing to hinder us; let us to work!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But, miserable man, where, where are we to do it?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: In the cave of Pan; nothing could be better.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But how to purify myself, before going back into the citadel?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Nothing easier! you can wash at the Clepsydra.[59]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But my oath? Do you want me to perjure myself?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I take all responsibility; never make yourself anxious.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, I'll be off, then, and find a bed for us.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! ’tis not worth while; we can lie on the ground surely.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No, no! bad man as you are, I don’t like your lying on the bare earth.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! how the dear girl loves me!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Myrrhiné (*coming back with a bed*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Come, get to bed quick; I am going to undress. But, plague take it, we must get a mattress.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: A mattress! Oh! no, never mind!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No, by Artemis! lie on the bare sacking, never! That were too squalid.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! by the great gods, be quick back!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Myrrhiné (*coming back with a mattress*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Here is a mattress. Lie down, I am just going to undress. But, but you’ve got no pillow.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! dear, oh, dear! they treat my poor penis for all the world like Heracles.[60]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Myrrhiné (*coming back with a pillow*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I am just unfastening my girdle. But remember what you promised me about making Peace; mind you keep your word.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, yes, upon my life I will.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Great Zeus! what matter of that? ’tis you I want to fuck.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Never fear—directly, directly! I’ll be back in no time.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: The woman will kill me with her blankets!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Myrrhiné (*coming back with a blanket*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But I tell you, our friend here is up—all stiff and ready!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Would you like me to scent you?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, by Aphrodité, but I will, whether you wish it or no.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! great Zeus, may she soon be done!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Myrrhiné (*coming back with a flask of perfume*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Hold out your hand; now rub it in.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! in Apollo’s name, I don’t much like the smell of it; but perhaps ’twill improve when it’s well rubbed in. It does not somehow smack of the marriage bed!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: There, what a scatterbrain I am; if I have not brought Rhodian perfumes![61]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Never mind, dearest, let be now.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Deuce take the man who first invented perfumes, say I!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Myrhhiné (*coming back with another flask*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I have a better all ready for your service, darling. Come, you provoking creature, to bed with you, and don’t bring another thing.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Coming, coming; I’m just slipping off my shoes. Dear boy, will you vote for peace?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I’ll think about it. (*Myrrhiné runs away*.) I’m a dead man, she is killing me! She has gone, and left me in torment! I must have someone to fuck, I must! Ah me! the loveliest of women has choused and cheated me. Poor little lad (*addressing his penis*), how am I to give you what you want so badly? Where is Cynalopex? quick, man, get him a nurse, do![62]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Poor, miserable wretch, baulked in your amorousness! what tortures are yours! Ah! you fill me with pity. Could any man’s back and loins stand such a strain? His organ stands stiff and rigid, and there’s never a wench to help him!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ye gods in heaven, what pains I suffer!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, there it is; ’tis her doing, that abandoned hussy!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Nay, nay! rather say that sweetest, dearest darling.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: That dearest darling? no, no, that hussy, say I! Zeus, thou god of the skies, canst not let loose a hurricane, to sweep them all up into the air, and whirl ’em round, then drop ’em down crash! and impale them on the point of his weapon!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Say, where shall I find the Senate and the Prytanes? I am bearer of despatches.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But are you a man or a Priapus, pray?[63]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! but he’s mighty simple. I am a herald, of course, I swear I am, and I come from Sparta about making peace.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But look, you are hiding a lance under your clothes, surely.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Then why do you turn away like that, and hold your cloak out from your body? Have you gotten swellings in the groin with your journey?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: By the twin brethren! the man’s an old maniac.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah, ha! my fine lad, why I can see it standing, oh fie!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I tell you no! but enough of this foolery.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, what is it you have there then?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh, indeed, a ‘skytalé,’ is it? Well, well, speak out frankly; I know all about these matters. How are things going at Sparta now?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Why, everything is turned upside down at Sparta; and all the allies are half dead with lusting. We simply must have Pellené.[65]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What is the reason of it all? Is it the god Pan’s doing?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No, but Lampito’s and the Spartan women’s, acting at her instigation; they have denied the men all access to their cunts.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: We are at our wits’ end; we walk bent double, just as if we were carrying lanterns in a wind. The jades have sworn we shall not so much as touch their cunts till we have all agreed to conclude peace.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ha, ha! So I see now, ’tis a general conspiracy embracing all Greece. Go you back to Sparta and bid them send Envoys with plenary powers to treat for peace. I will urge our Senators myself to name Plenipotentiaries from us; and to persuade them, why, I will show them this. (*Pointing to his erect penis*.)
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What could be better? I fly at your command.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No wild beast is there, no flame of fire, more fierce and untameable than woman; the panther is less savage and shameless.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And yet you dare to make war upon me, wretch, when you might have me for your most faithful friend and ally.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Never, never can my hatred cease towards women.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, please yourself. Still I cannot bear to leave you all naked as you are; folks would laugh at me. Come, I am going to put this tunic on you.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: You are right, upon my word! it was only in my confounded fit of rage I took it off.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Now at any rate you look like a man, and they won’t make fun of you. Ah! if you had not offended me so badly, I would take out that nasty insect you have in your eye for you.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! so that’s what was annoying me so! Look, here’s a ring, just remove the insect, and show it me. By Zeus! it has been hurting my eye this ever so long.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, I agree, though your manners are not over and above pleasant. Oh! what a huge great gnat! just look! It’s from Tricorysus, for sure.[66]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: A thousand thanks! the creature was digging a regular well in my eye; now it’s gone, my tears flow freely.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I will wipe them for you—bad, naughty man though you are. Now, just one kiss.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Just one, whether you like it or not.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! those confounded women! how they do cajole us! How true the saying: “’Tis impossible to live with the baggages, impossible to live without ’em”! Come, let us agree for the future not to regard each other any more as enemies; and to clinch the bargain, let us sing a choric song.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: We desire, Athenians, to speak ill of no man; but on the contrary to say much good of everyone, and to do the like. We have had enough of misfortunes and calamities. Is there any, man or woman, wants a bit of money—two or three minas or so;[67] well, our purse is full. If only peace is concluded, the borrower will not have to pay back. Also I’m inviting to supper a few Carystian friends,[68] who are excellently well qualified. I have still a drop of good soup left, and a young porker I’m going to kill, and the flesh will be sweet and tender. I shall expect you at my house to-day; but first away to the baths with you, you and your children; then come all of you, ask no one’s leave, but walk straight up, as if you were at home; never fear, the door will be . . . shut in your faces![69]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! here come the Envoys from Sparta with their long flowing beards; why, you would think they wore a cage[70] between their thighs. (*Enter the Lacedæmonian Envoys*.) Hail to you, first of all, Laconians; then tell us how you fare.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No need for many words; you see what a state we are in.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Alas! the situation grows more and more strained! the intensity of the thing is just frightful.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: ’Tis beyond belief. But to work! summon your Commissioners, and let us patch up the best peace we may.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! our men too, like wrestlers in the arena, cannot endure a rag over their bellies; ’tis an athlete’s malady, which only exercise can remedy.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Can anybody tell us where Lysistrata is? Surely she will have some compassion on our condition.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Look! ’tis the very same complaint. (*Addressing the Athenian*.) Don’t you feel of mornings a strong nervous tension?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, and a dreadful, dreadful torture it is! Unless peace is made very soon, we shall find no resource but to fuck Clisthenes.[71]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Take my advice, and put on your clothes again; one of the fellows who mutilated the Hermæ[72] might see you.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Quite right. There, I will slip on my tunic.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! what a terrible state we are in! Greeting to you, Laconian fellow-sufferers.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Laconian (*addressing one of his countrymen*).
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! my boy, what a thing it would have been if these fellows had seen us just now when our tools were on full stand!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Speak out, Laconians, what is it brings you here?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: We have come to treat for peace.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well said; we are of the same mind. Better call Lysistrata then; she is the only person will bring us to terms.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, yes—and Lysistratus into the bargain, if you will.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Needless to call her; she has heard your voices, and here she comes.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Hail, boldest and bravest of womankind! The time is come to show yourself in turn uncompromising and conciliatory, exacting and yielding, haughty and condescending. Call up all your skill and artfulness. Lo! the foremost men in Hellas, seduced by your fascinations, are agreed to entrust you with the task of ending their quarrels.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: ’Twill be an easy task—if only they refrain from mutual indulgence in masculine love; if they do, I shall know the fact at once. Now, where is the gentle goddess Peace? Lead hither the Laconian Envoys. But, look you, no roughness or violence; our husbands always behaved so boorishly.[73] Bring them to me with smiles, as women should. If any refuse to give you his hand, then catch him by the penis and draw him politely forward. Bring up the Athenians too; you may take them just how you will. Laconians, approach; and you, Athenians, on my other side. Now hearken all! I am but a woman; but I have good common sense; Nature has dowered me with discriminating judgment, which I have yet further developed, thanks to the wise teachings of my father and the elders of the city. First I must bring a reproach against you that applies equally to both sides. At Olympia, and Thermopylæ, and Delphi, and a score of other places too numerous to mention, you celebrate before the same altars ceremonies common to all Hellenes; yet you go cutting each other’s throats, and sacking Hellenic cities, when all the while the Barbarian is yonder threatening you! That is my first point.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah, ah! concupiscence is killing me!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Now ’tis to you I address myself, Laconians. Have you forgotten how Periclides,[74] your own countryman, sat a suppliant before our altars? How pale he was in his purple robes! He had come to crave an army of us; ’twas the time when Messenia was pressing you sore, and the Sea-god was shaking the earth. Cimon marched to your aid at the head of four thousand hoplites, and saved Lacedæmon. And, after such a service as that, you ravage the soil of your benefactors!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: They do wrong, very wrong, Lysistrata.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: We do wrong, very wrong. Ah! great gods! what lovely thighs she has!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And now a word to the Athenians. Have you no memory left of how, in the days when ye wore the tunic of slaves, the Laconians came, spear in hand, and slew a host of Thessalians and partisans of Hippias the Tyrant? They, and they only, fought on your side on that eventful day; they delivered you from despotism, and thanks to them our Nation could change the short tunic of the slave for the long cloak of the free man.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I have never seen a woman of more gracious dignity.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: I have never seen a woman with a finer cunt!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Bound by such ties of mutual kindness, how can you bear to be at war? Stop, stay the hateful strife, be reconciled; what hinders you?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: We are quite ready, if they will give us back our rampart.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Pylos, which we have been asking for and craving for ever so long.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: In the Sea-god’s name, you shall never have it!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But then what city shall we be able to stir up trouble in?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ask for another place in exchange.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah! that’s the ticket! Well, to begin with, give us Echinus, the Maliac gulf adjoining, and the two legs of Megara.[75]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh! surely, surely not all that, my dear sir.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Come to terms; never make a difficulty of two legs more or less!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, I’m ready now to off coat and cultivate my land.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And I too, to dung it to start with.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: That’s just what you shall do, once peace is signed. So, if you really want to make it, go consult your allies about the matter.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: What allies, I should like to know? Why, we are all on the stand; not one but is mad to be fucking. What we all want, is to be abed with our wives; how should our allies fail to second our project?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: And ours the same, for certain sure!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: The Carystians first and foremost, by the gods!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well said, indeed! Now be off to purify yourselves for entering the Acropolis, where the women invite you to supper; we will empty our provision baskets to do you honour. At table, you will exchange oaths and pledges; then each man will go home with his wife.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Come along then, and as quick as may be.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Quick, quick’s the word, say I.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Embroidered stuffs, and dainty tunics, and flowing gowns, and golden ornaments, everything I have, I offer them you with all my heart; take them all for your children, for your girls, against they are chosen “basket-bearers” to the goddess. I invite you every one to enter, come in and choose whatever you will; there is nothing so well fastened, you cannot break the seals, and carry away the contents. Look about you everywhere . . . you won’t find a blessed thing, unless you have sharper eyes than mine.\* And if any of you lacks corn to feed his slaves and his young and numerous family, why, I have a few grains of wheat at home; let him take what I have to give, a big twelve-pound loaf included. So let my poorer neighbours all come with bags and wallets; my man, Manes, shall give them corn; but I warn them not to come near my door, or—beware the dog![76]
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Go your way, I tell you. Why, bless me, they’re sitting down now; I shall have to singe ’em with my torch to make ’em stir! What an impudent lot of fellows!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well, as you *must* stop, and I don’t want to offend you—but you’ll see some queer sights.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Well and good, I’ve no objection.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: No, no, you must be off—or I’ll tear your hair out, I will; be off, I say, and don’t annoy the Laconian Envoys; they’re just coming out from the banquet-hall.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Such a merry banquet I’ve never seen before! The Laconians were simply charming. After the drink is in, why, we’re all wise men, all. It’s only natural, to be sure, for sober, we’re all fools. Take my advice, my fellow-countrymen, our Envoys should always be drunk. We go to Sparta; we enter the city sober; why, we must be picking a quarrel directly. We don’t understand what they say to us, we imagine a lot they don’t say at all, and we report home all wrong, all topsy-turvy. But, look you, to-day it’s quite different; we’re enchanted whatever happens; instead of Clitagoras, they might sing us Telamon,[77] and we should clap our hands just the same. A perjury or two into the bargain, la! what does that matter to merry companions in their cups?
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: But here they are back again! Will you begone, you loafing scoundrels.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Ah ha! here’s the company coming out already.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: My dear, sweet friend, come, take your flute in hand; I would fain dance and sing my best in honour of the Athenians and our noble selves.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Yes, take your flute, i’ the gods’ name. What a delight to see him dance!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Oh Mnemosyné! inspire these men, inspire my muse who knows our exploits and those of the Athenians. With what a godlike ardour did they swoop down at Artemisium[78] on the ships of the Medes! What a glorious victory was that! For the soldiers of Leonidas,[79] they were like fierce wild-boars whetting their tushes. The sweat ran down their faces, and drenched all their limbs, for verily the Persians were as many as the sands of the seashore. Oh! Artemis, huntress queen, whose arrows pierce the denizens of the woods, virgin goddess, be thou favourable to the Peace we here conclude; through thee may our hearts be long united! May this treaty draw close for ever the bonds of a happy friendship! No more wiles and stratagems! Aid us, oh! aid us, maiden huntress!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: All is for the best; and now, Laconians, take your wives away home with you, and you, Athenians, yours. May husband live happily with wife, and wife with husband. Dance, dance, to celebrate our bliss, and let us be heedful to avoid like mistakes for the future.
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Appear, appear, dancers, and the Graces with you! Let us invoke, one and all, Artemis, and her heavenly brother, gracious Apollo, patron of the dance, and Dionysus, whose eye darts flame, as he steps forward surrounded by the Mænad maids, and Zeus, who wields the flashing lightning, and his august, thrice-blessed spouse, the Queen of Heaven! These let us invoke, and all the other gods, calling all the inhabitants of the skies to witness the noble Peace now concluded under the fond auspices of Aphrodité. Io Pæan! Io Pæan! dance, leap, as in honour of a victory won. Evoé! Evoé! And you, our Laconian guests, sing us a new and inspiring strain!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses

passages.text: Leave once more, oh! leave once more the noble height of Taygetus, oh! Muse of Lacedæmon, and join us in singing the praises of Apollo of Amyclæ, and Athena of the Brazen House, and the gallant twin sons of Tyndarus, who practise arms on the banks of Eurotas river.[80] Haste, haste hither with nimble-footed pace, let us sing Sparta, the city that delights in choruses divinely sweet and graceful dances, when our maidens bound lightly by the river side, like frolicsome fillies, beating the ground with rapid steps and shaking their long locks in the wind, as Bacchantes wave their wands in the wild revels of the Wine-god. At their head, oh! chaste and beauteous goddess, daughter of Latona, Artemis, do thou lead the song and dance. A fillet binding thy waving tresses, appear in thy loveliness; leap like a fawn; strike thy divine hands together to animate the dance, and aid us to renown the valiant goddess of battles, great Athené of the Brazen House!
passages.locusKind: Wikisource dialogue blocks; unaligned to Greek verses
